Ethereum - A Distributed Computer - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A developer says Ethereum is mainly Bitcoin with a different native coin. Which response best reflects how Ethereum is actually designed?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum uses a blockchain as a shared execution platform where smart contracts can hold value, update state, and enforce application logic.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum mainly records ether payments while smart contract rules run as wallet-side scripts outside the shared consensus process.
Ethereum gives each application its own isolated ledger so contract rules can differ without being verified by the wider network.
Ethereum extends Bitcoin with richer transaction templates, while persistent contract state is managed by separate off-chain services.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames Ethereum as a shift from blockchain-as-digital-money to blockchain-as-shared-computer: common execution semantics let many applications share one replicated state machine.
questions.lesson_block: From Digital Money To Shared Computation
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Beyond Cryptocurrency: Buterin's Vision; From Digital Money To Shared Computation

questions.question_stem: An ERC standard has been publicly specified and discussed, but major wallets and applications have not adopted it. What is its practical effect?
questions.correct_answer: The specification alone does not make it binding; practical impact depends on implementation, testing, and opt-in adoption by ecosystem participants.
incorrect_answers: The ERC becomes a de facto protocol rule once the proposal number is assigned, requiring wallets to support the interface before testing.
Core developers can activate the ERC through client releases, so application teams must treat it as consensus immediately after publication.
Validators enforce the ERC as part of block validity, so tokens using older interfaces are rejected even if their contract code has not changed.
questions.explanation: Ethereum governance is social and operational. EIPs and ERCs matter when client teams, validators, node operators, applications, wallets, exchanges, and users coordinate around them.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Governance & Ethereum Improvement Proposals (EIPs); EIP Workflow; Stakeholders & Decision Making

questions.question_stem: Why would a smart contract that directly reads a validator's local clock or fetches a website during execution threaten Ethereum consensus?
questions.correct_answer: Different nodes could observe different values, causing them to compute different state transitions from the same transaction.
incorrect_answers: Those values would make signatures invalid, because validators sign a transaction only after the contract has finished running.
The contract would spend extra gas for the website request, but consensus would still agree as long as the response is cached.
The issue is mainly privacy: a validator clock reveals metadata, while the state transition remains identical everywhere.
questions.explanation: Ethereum requires deterministic execution: the same prior state and transaction input must produce the same result everywhere. Local clocks, network calls, and OS randomness break that property.
questions.lesson_block: EVM, Determinism, And Gas As The Execution Foundation
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM); Determinism & Execution Constraints

questions.question_stem: What is the best explanation for why Ethereum uses gas instead of trying to prove ahead of time that every contract execution will finish?
questions.correct_answer: Because general halt prediction is undecidable, Ethereum meters execution and stops computation when the transaction's gas budget is exhausted.
incorrect_answers: Because contract authors can usually estimate loop bounds, Ethereum verifies source code during deployment and uses gas mainly to recover validator costs.
Because validators can simulate every possible branch before inclusion, Ethereum uses gas chiefly to divide execution fees among network participants.
Because Turing-complete code is converted into fixed-length bytecode, Ethereum uses gas to schedule execution order rather than to bound computation.
questions.explanation: The lesson connects expressive smart-contract code to the Halting Problem. Gas bounds computation, prices resource use, and protects the network from unbounded execution.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: The Halting Problem; Gas: Metering Computation and Storage

questions.question_stem: A transaction calls a contract, updates storage temporarily, then runs out of gas before completion. What outcome should a student expect?
questions.correct_answer: The storage changes from that execution are reverted, but the sender still pays for computation already consumed.
incorrect_answers: The contract's earlier storage writes remain in state, and unused gas is refunded once execution stops at the limit.
The contract returns the last successful intermediate state, while the sender loses only the unused gas for execution.
The failed call is excluded from the block, but the sender still pays a fixed fee for the attempted contract execution.
questions.explanation: Out-of-gas execution reverts state changes to preserve atomicity, but gas consumed before failure is still charged because the network spent resources executing the transaction.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Gas: Metering Computation and Storage; Common Misconceptions And Confusions

questions.question_stem: A crop-insurance contract needs to pay out when rainfall falls below a threshold. What new issue appears when an oracle supplies the rainfall data?
questions.correct_answer: The contract now depends on assumptions about the oracle's data quality, honesty, manipulation resistance, and availability.
incorrect_answers: The oracle makes the rainfall fact deterministic on-chain, so the remaining risk is whether users accept the payout schedule.
The contract can verify sensor signatures, so it no longer needs assumptions about who selected and maintained the weather stations.
The data feed moves execution off Ethereum, so validators no longer re-run the contract payout logic before accepting a block.
questions.explanation: Oracles bridge the gap between deterministic on-chain execution and off-chain facts, but they do not make external reality trustless. They shift trust to data providers and reporting mechanisms.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Oracles: Bridging Blockchains and Reality; Boundaries Of On-Chain Knowledge

questions.question_stem: Which scenario correctly distinguishes externally owned accounts from contract accounts in Ethereum?
questions.correct_answer: An EOA is controlled by a private key and initiates a transaction, while a contract account contains code and storage that execute only when called.
incorrect_answers: An EOA has no contract code and signs transactions with a private key, while a contract account can initiate transactions whenever its code schedules them.
A contract account stores bytecode and persistent storage, while an EOA stores no code but can be triggered only by another contract call.
An EOA pays gas through a wallet signature, while a contract account must be controlled by a validator-selected private key before its code can run.
questions.explanation: EOAs initiate transactions and pay gas through private-key control. Contract accounts are code and storage at addresses and run when invoked by transactions or other contract calls.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Accounts & Global State (EOA vs Contract); From EVM to Programs - Smart Contracts

questions.question_stem: Why does Ethereum's account model fit persistent smart-contract applications better than Bitcoin's UTXO model?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum can update mutable account balances and contract storage directly, which supports repeated interaction with long-lived program state.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum turns each contract call into a fresh UTXO record, which makes prior contract state easier to reconstruct from spent outputs.
Ethereum accounts keep contract code and storage under addresses, but each update still consumes one-time outputs like Bitcoin payments.
Ethereum avoids storing long-lived program state on-chain, so applications rebuild balances from event logs instead of updating contract storage directly.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts Ethereum's mutable account balances and contract storage with Bitcoin's UTXO model. Persistent storage makes repeated stateful application logic more natural.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: Transaction Models: UTXO vs Accounts; Accounts & Global State (EOA vs Contract)

questions.question_stem: A user worries that The Merge restarted Ethereum and reset deployed contracts. Which answer best corrects that misconception?
questions.correct_answer: The Merge changed block production from proof-of-work mining to proof-of-stake validation while preserving users, balances, contracts, and application state.
incorrect_answers: The Merge kept user balances but moved contract storage into PoS addresses, so applications had to migrate state through upgrade scripts after activation.
The Merge changed the EVM and consensus together, preserving ether balances while requiring deployed contracts to recompile under proof-of-stake.
The Merge left deployed contracts readable but paused state-changing calls until validators re-created application state under proof-of-stake checkpoints.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats The Merge as a consensus-layer transition, not an application-layer restart. It changed how blocks are produced and finalized while preserving the application state.

questions.question_stem: In Ethereum's modular scaling roadmap, why is simply making L1 blocks much larger treated as a risky solution?
questions.correct_answer: Larger blocks can raise hardware, bandwidth, storage, and sync requirements, reducing broad verifiability and pressuring decentralization.
incorrect_answers: Larger blocks would make gas metering unnecessary for contract execution, so the protocol would lose its normal resource bound during validation.
Larger blocks mainly weaken rollups by making L2 data unavailable, even when ordinary nodes can still verify L1 cheaply from home.
Larger blocks would let the EVM execute rollup data directly, replacing the need for separate L2 execution, settlement, and data availability layers.
questions.explanation: The lesson's scaling argument emphasizes verifiability. Ethereum keeps L1 focused on consensus, ordering, settlement, and data availability while L2s move much execution off L1.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_01-EF-ethereum_intro-slides-only.qmd: State Growth & Storage Pressure; The Scaling Problem; Modular Scaling

questions.question_stem: According to the Ethereum whitepaper, what is the key design motivation for Ethereum compared with launching a separate blockchain for each application?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum provides a shared general-purpose state transition platform so applications can define logic without bootstrapping separate consensus and networking.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum was designed to make each application inherit Bitcoin UTXO validation rules, avoiding separate consensus while keeping contract logic off-chain.
Ethereum offered a common scripting layer for application-specific chains, so developers could reuse EVM code while still launching independent consensus networks.
Ethereum treated the blockchain mostly as a payments ledger and expected complex applications to run through external meta-protocol clients instead of shared execution.
questions.explanation: The whitepaper argues that once blockchains provide decentralized ordering, a generalized execution layer can host many applications instead of forcing every application to create a new chain or constrained meta-protocol.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/ethereum_whitepaper.txt: Ethereum; Alternative Blockchain Applications; Why Bitcoin-Layer Alternatives Were Not Enough

questions.question_stem: An EOA sends a transaction to a contract, and that contract calls a second contract before returning a result. Which Ethereum concept does this best illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Messages allow contracts to interact with other contracts, making contract accounts composable actors in Ethereum applications.
incorrect_answers: Internal messages can move ether, but they cannot carry call data or invoke another contract during the same transaction.
Contract accounts can run background loops between blocks, which lets the second contract respond without being triggered by a call.
The first contract temporarily becomes an EOA, signing a nested transaction to authorize the second contract call before returning.
questions.explanation: The reading distinguishes signed external transactions from messages generated during execution. Contract-to-contract messages can carry value and data, return responses, and compose applications.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/ethereum_whitepaper.txt: Ethereum Accounts; Messages and Transactions; Accounts, Messages, And Composability

questions.question_stem: Transaction fees on Ethereum are not merely a private payment from sender to block producer. Why?
questions.correct_answer: Every included transaction imposes verification, processing, and download costs on the wider network, so fees help regulate shared resource use.
incorrect_answers: The block proposer is the main actor that executes transactions, so fees chiefly compensate proposer hardware and bandwidth costs.
Fees are set by wallet policy after execution, so they mainly measure payment priority rather than validation and download work imposed on nodes.
Gas prices reimburse validator opportunity cost for failed transactions, while successful transfers are verified locally by wallets.
questions.explanation: The reading treats fees and gas as network-resource regulation. Transaction inclusion creates costs for validating nodes, which creates abuse and tragedy-of-the-commons concerns if costs are not priced.
